title: The Medicine Buddha's mantra

lines: A BUDDHA THE COLOR OF LAPIS.
cards: On the wall of a Tibetan clinic or a family shrine, there's sometimes a painting of a buddha who looks different from the others. His body is deep blue, the blue of lapis lazuli.
In his left hand, resting in his lap, is a bowl. In his right, held out toward you, a branch with a small fruit. The bowl isn't for alms.
He's holding medicine. Some people chant his mantra at hospital bedsides, and some keep it running quietly on their own bad days. You met him in his sutra on day eleven ninety-nine.

teach.b: First, who he is. His Sanskrit name, Bhaishajyaguru, is usually translated medicine teacher.
A sutra about him tells how, long ago, as a bodhisattva, he vowed that those who are sick, poor or without help would be relieved when they hear his name. Second, the mantra.
In Sanskrit: tadyatha om bhaishajye bhaishajye mahabhaishajye raja samudgate svaha. In Tibetan it's often said: teyata om bekandze bekandze maha bekandze radza samungate soha.
You can hear the word for medicine in it, called twice, then called great. Third, two kinds of sickness. The mantra is chanted for bodies: a fever, a diagnosis, a friend in surgery.
Teachers also point to a deeper illness Buddhist teaching names, the three poisons of greed, hatred and delusion. The medicine in the bowl, they say, is for both.
Tibetan medical tradition even presents its root medical text as taught by the Medicine Buddha.
Fourth, alongside care, not instead of it. The same tradition that honors him built a whole system of medicine, with doctors and remedies.
The chant belongs beside that care: it steadies the mind, gathers compassion and sends good wishes, while the body gets real treatment. And so it often turns outward.
It's said for healing, wherever it's needed.

how: Tibetan Buddhists recite the Medicine Buddha's mantra for the sick, for the dying and for their own health, often with a visualization of the blue Medicine Buddha, and Medicine Buddha practices are held for people who are ill.

games.q: what does “the medicine buddha's mantra” mean?
o: a cure that replaces doctors and medical treatment
a chant to the blue buddha of healing, for body and mind
a spell said only by Tibetan doctors, never lay people

games.q: the Medicine Buddha: tap the pairs.

s: the mantra is meant to replace going to a doctor
the same tradition built a system of medicine; the mantra is said alongside care.
the Medicine Buddha is often painted deep blue, holding a bowl of medicine
the mantra is only ever said for yourself
it's often said for others: at bedsides, for friends, for anyone unwell.

games.q: someone you love is sick. you've just learned the Medicine Buddha's mantra. what fits the way the tradition uses it?
o: chant it instead of seeing a doctor.
chant it, or wish them well, alongside real care.
keep it for yourself, since they're the one who's sick.
games.why: the chant steadies the mind and sends good wishes while the body gets real treatment. alongside care, not instead of it.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is unwell, in body or in spirit; if it's you, that's allowed.

If you'd like, picture a deep blue light like the Medicine Buddha's resting over them, calm and steady, and silently, in your own plain words, wish that they heal, that their pain eases, that they're cared for.
If you know the mantra and it's yours to say, you can say it softly.

wordCard.voice: The Medicine Buddha's mantra. A chant to the blue buddha of healing, said for bodies and for the deeper sickness of the mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit Bhaishajyaguru: the Medicine Buddha, usually translated 'medicine teacher'.

carryVoice: Your line: for healing. For bodies, and for the mind's deeper sickness too. See you tomorrow.
